titleOriginal: 商务部、海关总署公告2025年第18号
titleEn: MOFCOM & GACC Announcement No. 18 of 2025: export controls on certain medium and heavy rare-earth-related items
summary: China's Ministry of Commerce and the General Administration of Customs jointly imposed export licensing on seven medium and heavy rare earths — samarium, gadolinium, terbium, dysprosium, lutetium, scandium and yttrium — together with their oxides, alloys, compounds and mixtures, and related magnets. Exporters must obtain MOFCOM licenses; the measure is a licensing regime, not an outright ban.
analyticalSignificance: The opening move of the 2025 escalation, announced days after new US tariffs. Beijing targeted the medium and heavy rare earths where its separation monopoly is most complete, demonstrating chokepoint leverage while framing the step in standard control terms rather than as retaliation. These April controls have remained in force throughout the later expansion and suspension.

issuingBody: MOFCOM (Bureau of Industrial Security and Import and Export Controls)
titleOriginal: 商务部公告2025第61号 公布对境外相关稀土物项实施出口管制的决定
titleEn: MOFCOM Announcement No. 61 of 2025: Decision to Implement Controls on Exports of Rare Earth-Related Items to Foreign Countries
summary: MOFCOM expanded the regime, adding five further rare earths (holmium, erbium, thulium, europium, ytterbium) and, most significantly, asserting extraterritorial jurisdiction: foreign-made items containing 0.1% or more by value of Chinese-origin controlled rare earths — or produced using Chinese rare-earth extraction, separation, metal-smelting, magnet-making or recycling technology — would require a license. Companion measures covered related technology and equipment.
analyticalSignificance: The extraterritorial 0.1% rule mirrors the design of US export controls (a de minimis / foreign-direct-product logic) and marks a qualitative escalation from controlling exports of Chinese material to controlling foreign goods derived from it. This is the measure later suspended under the November 2025 stand-down.

titleEn: MOFCOM announcement suspending the 9 October 2025 rare-earth export-control measures (to 10 November 2026)
summary: Following the Busan leaders' meeting, MOFCOM announced (7 November 2025, effective 10 November 2025) a one-year suspension of the 9 October 2025 measures, running to 10 November 2026. The earlier 4 April 2025 controls on the original seven elements were not suspended and remain in force.
analyticalSignificance: Confirms that the October escalation functioned as negotiating leverage that could be switched off — but the suspension is time-bound and reversible, not a repeal, and leaves the April baseline intact. The original-language announcement text has not yet been transcribed for this record; the document number is therefore left null pending verification against the primary.

summary: The USGS, through the Department of the Interior, finalized the 2025 List of Critical Minerals: 60 minerals in total, with ten added in 2025 (boron, copper, lead, metallurgical coal, phosphate, potash, rhenium, silicon, silver and uranium) on the basis of new data, public feedback and interagency recommendations. Designation drives permitting priority, funding eligibility and supply-chain attention; it is not itself an export control.
analyticalSignificance: The principal US instrument is designation, paired with funding and offtake — the mirror image of China's control-and-license posture. Several 2025 additions (notably copper, metallurgical coal and uranium) reflect interagency and executive direction that goes beyond the USGS quantitative screening methodology, signalling a more security-driven definition of 'critical'.

issuingBody: European Parliament and Council / European Commission
titleOriginal: Regulation (EU) 2024/1252 establishing a framework for ensuring a secure and sustainable supply of critical raw materials
titleEn: Regulation (EU) 2024/1252 establishing a framework for ensuring a secure and sustainable supply of critical raw materials (Critical Raw Materials Act)
summary: The Critical Raw Materials Act entered into force on 23 May 2024. It sets 2030 benchmarks for the EU's annual consumption of strategic raw materials — at least 10% extracted, 40% processed and 25% recycled domestically, and no more than 65% from any single third country — and creates Strategic Project designations with accelerated permitting. The first Strategic Projects were designated in 2025.
analyticalSignificance: The EU instrument is benchmark-and-designation: de-risking through diversification targets rather than export leverage. It predates the April 2025 acute phase and is included as the standing framework the 2025 Chinese measures act upon. It anchors the EU's 'de-risking, not decoupling' posture.

titleOriginal: DoD–MP Materials public-private partnership for rare earth magnet supply
titleEn: DoD–MP Materials public-private partnership for rare earth magnet supply
summary: DoD agreed to buy $400M of newly created MP Materials preferred stock plus a 10-year warrant at $30.03/share, positioning it to become the largest shareholder (~15%); added a $150M loan, a 10-year NdPr price floor of $110/kg, and a 10-year magnet offtake commitment, to build domestic separation and magnet capacity at Mountain Pass and a second magnet plant.
analyticalSignificance: Marks a shift to direct US equity-and-price-floor industrial policy in rare earths, explicitly to reduce dependence on China; read as the US emulating state-backed models it long avoided.

issuingBody: Department of Industry, Science and Resources
titleOriginal: Critical Minerals Strategic Reserve — initial minerals
titleEn: Critical Minerals Strategic Reserve — initial minerals
summary: Australia named rare earths, antimony, and gallium as the initial focus of its A$1.2B Critical Minerals Strategic Reserve (committed by PM Albanese on 24 April 2025, in the 2025-26 budget, operational from H2 2026). The reserve secures rights to Australian-produced minerals and on-sells them to allies, drawing on the expanded A$5B Critical Minerals Facility and Export Finance Australia offtake powers.
analyticalSignificance: A demand-side allied counter to Chinese concentration, framed around supplying partners (Canada, Japan, Europe, UK); follows the October 2025 US-Australia rare earths framework.

titleOriginal: JARE additional equity investment in Lynas and heavy rare earth offtake
titleEn: JARE additional equity investment in Lynas and heavy rare earth offtake
summary: Japan Australia Rare Earth (JARE), the Sojitz–JOGMEC vehicle, committed a further A$200M of equity to Lynas to fund light-REE expansion and the start of heavy-REE (dysprosium, terbium) separation, with an agreement to take up to 65% of the heavy REEs produced. Builds on JOGMEC's decade-plus backing of Lynas since the 2010 Chinese rare-earth shock; Sojitz began importing Lynas-separated Dy/Tb in October 2025, the first operational heavy-REE chain outside China.
analyticalSignificance: The clearest long-run example of patient state-backed offtake-plus-equity to build non-Chinese heavy-REE supply, the chokepoint China most dominates.

issuingBody: Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada
titleOriginal: ICA divestiture order — three Chinese investors in critical-mineral firms
titleEn: ICA divestiture order — three Chinese investors in critical-mineral firms
summary: Under the Investment Canada Act, Canada ordered three Chinese investors to divest holdings in Canadian critical-mineral juniors (Sinomine from Power Metals, Chengze Lithium from Lithium Chile, Zangge Mining from Ultra Lithium), days after a 28 October 2022 policy making SOE investment in critical minerals approvable only "on an exceptional basis." Affected minerals include lithium, cesium, and tantalum, none of which are in the v1 material set.
analyticalSignificance: A leading allied use of investment screening (rather than export control) as a critical-minerals instrument, tied to friend-shoring rhetoric and timed alongside US engagement.

titleOriginal: 商务部 海关总署公告2023年第23号 关于对镓、锗相关物项实施出口管制的公告
titleEn: MOFCOM/GACC Announcement No. 23 of 2023 on export controls on gallium- and germanium-related items
summary: Effective 1 August 2023, eight gallium-related and six germanium-related items require a dual-use export license from provincial MOFCOM (not a ban). First major Chinese critical-material control of this cycle, days after expanded US/allied semiconductor controls.
analyticalSignificance: Established the licensing template (end-use/end-user disclosure, roughly 60-day review) reused in later controls; exports to the US fell to near zero.

titleEn: MOFCOM/GACC Announcement No. 39 of 2023 on graphite export control measures
summary: Effective 1 December 2023, three high-sensitivity synthetic and natural-flake graphite categories moved onto the dual-use control list; five low-sensitivity items were de-controlled. Replaced the 2006 temporary graphite regime.
analyticalSignificance: Targeted EV-battery anode supply; stated justification cited national security and non-proliferation obligations. Original-language text and a quoted framing anchor are not yet coded for this record.

titleEn: MOFCOM Announcement No. 46 of 2024 on strengthening export controls of dual-use items to the United States
summary: Issued one day after a US BIS action adding ~140 entities and tightening chip controls, this barred, in principle, exports to the US of gallium, germanium, antimony, and superhard materials, prohibited all dual-use exports to US military end users/uses, and tightened graphite end-use review. The materials ban (Article 2) was suspended by MOFCOM Announcement No. 72 of 2025, effective to 27 November 2026; the Article 1 military-end-use prohibition was not addressed.
analyticalSignificance: The clearest country-specific retaliatory escalation of the cycle, converting licensing into an outright US-directed ban. The retaliation reading rests on the one-day-after-BIS timing and lives here, not in the quoted anchor, which states the national-security and non-proliferation justification.

titleEn: MOFCOM/GACC Announcement No. 10 of 2025 on export controls on tungsten and related items
summary: Added tungsten, tellurium, bismuth, molybdenum, and indium-related items to the dual-use export control list, requiring licenses. Only tungsten is in the v1 material set; the others are noted here, not coded as materials.
analyticalSignificance: Extended controls into defense-relevant refractory metals where China holds a dominant processing share. The original-language text and a quoted framing anchor are not yet coded.
